entries.title: November Bookmarks: A Single Woman in a Dust-Proof Room
entries.summary: A selection of passages we underlined in new releases this November.
entries.content:
Emma Eaton

Bookmarks

Each month, our desks at the Review pile up with dozens of soon-to-be published books. This November, in addition to translator Jennifer Croft’s memoir Notes on Postcards and From Julio, a volume of Julio Cortázar’s selected letters, we read a political thriller-cum-radio broadcast about a Ukrainian barricade pianist. Sometimes, looking through these galleys for invention or inspiration, I keep a few passages for myself. Here’s what struck me lately. 

—Emma Eaton, editorial intern

The German poet Ernst Herbeck, who was institutionalized for schizophrenia at twenty, began writing poems at the encouragement of his clinician. He often wrote in response to a prompt, which would then form his title. This poem, from Herbeck’s In His One Languages (World Poetry), translated from the German by David Brazil and Gary Sullivan, is called “The Cigarette.”

The Cigarette.



is a monopoly and must

be smoked. So Thatit

goes up in flames.

*

Mark Danner’s Crossing the Rubicon: The Betrayal of American Democracy, 2000–2026 (NYRB) offers a comprehensive collection of the writer’s essays from Bush v. Gore to the second Trump administration. From an essay on Obama: 

He seems slender and slight and young, astonishingly young, and you notice first of all, for it is impossible not to, the physical grace; he moves like an athlete much more than a politician, taking pleasure in his body: bursting up onto the stage, the lanky highly stylized movement, shoulders bent slightly concave, gathering everything into those constantly clapping hands, using the hands in their clapping to acknowledge the crowd, his head nodding all the while, as if he is drawing his energy only from them and showing that energy with his clapping and nodding, with the bursting energy of his body that is an embodiment of theirs, an embodied picture of what they’re giving him. He prances with evident pleasure around the little stage, moving his head in big theatrical nods, embracing each politician in turn, big full-bodied embraces, and again one thinks of an athlete on the sidelines or in the dugout: all of it is done with the unhindered pleasure of the body, all of it says confidence and pleasure, as if this, being bathed in the huge cheers, taking sustenance and energy from the wave of sounds and the shouts of his name, is the place where he breathes his true oxygen, where he really lives. He seems made to be precisely here—in the midst of these thousands of sundrenched cheering people.

*

Simon Garfield’s The Pen: A Human History (Crown) introduces us to the characters of pen history, from Joseph Priestley—the eighteenth-century scientist who, in addition to discovering oxygen, was the first person to shove a metal nib onto a quill—to Milton Reynolds, the millionaire inventor of the Reynolds Rocket, the worlds’ first ballpoint pen. In this scene, he’s visiting Axel Nier, “nib specialist”: 

Towards the end of my time in Nibs, my eye was drawn to a single woman in a dust-proof room writing figure eights. This room was known as The Aquarium and was the final stage; the woman was testing nibs for resistance, smoothness and flow, and also sound. “The ideal sound is hard to understand,” Nier explained to me quietly, “but she knows.”

*

The Polish futurist Aleksander Wat wrote his diary primarily in an invented and vowel-less code of his own invention. The loose-leaf papers on which his entries were typed were found after Wat’s death in 1967. NYRB’s new collection of the entries, Diary Without Vowels (NYRB), translated from the Polish by Alissa Valles, does include some vowels:

November 7, 1963

How strong I was today, how resilient, though the day was rather cold and windy, and my pains were mild, despite all the nerves, efforts, and worries.

*

Some more weather in Siamak Vossoughi’s The Friend Seekers (Sarabande Books), the author’s third book of short stories:

It was a Saturday afternoon and the sky was gray in a way that seemed like Saturday afternoon was always going to be gray from here on out.

*

A passage from Yuri Andrukhovych’s Radio Night (NYRB), translated from the Ukrainian by Mark Andryczyk:

Lady Gaga was heading for Rotsky with such unwavering aim (while limping, no less) that he didn’t have the least bit of doubt: he would now be offered drugs.

Emma Eaton is an editorial intern at The Paris Review.

entries.title: Threads of Imagery: Barbara Trapido’s Debut Novel Forty Years On
entries.summary: “It is a novel about how to live, or how to be: how to be happy, how to be sad, how to fall in love, how to collapse in a heap when love doesn’t work out.”
entries.content:
Rosa Lyster

One Book

Barbara Trapido’s Brother of the More Famous Jack, originally published in 1982 and reissued this year by New York Review Books, opens with its young heroine, Katherine, reading the preface of a book written by her beloved professor, Jacob Goldman:

I cannot in good conscience give the statutory thanks to my wife for helpful comments on the manuscript, patient reading of drafts or corrections to proofs, because Jane did none of these things … Going by the lavish thanks to wives which I find in the prefaces to other men’s books, I deem myself uniquely injudicious in having married a woman who refuses to double as a high-grade editorial assistant. Since custom requires me to thank her for something, I thank her instead for the agreeable fact of her continuing presence which in twenty years I have never presumed to expect.

“There is no doubt,” says Katherine, that the preface—the marriage it speaks of and the world it hints at—“influenced the paths that I chose to tread.” There are many people who would probably say the same of Brother of the More Famous Jack. I read it for the first time when I was sixteen; now, decades later, I find it nearly impossible to disentangle some of my own tastes and preferences from those expressed in the novel. Do I think that having revolting handwriting is glamorous because of Brother of the More Famous Jack, or would I have gotten there on my own? Do I think wearing an all-white outfit to play amateur tennis is embarrassing because of the novel, or does that kind of thing become obvious to all adults eventually? I began rereading the novel in preparation for this interview and realized almost immediately that I didn’t need to: I had the whole thing more or less off by heart.

It is a novel about how to live, or how to be: how to be happy, how to be sad, how to fall in love, how to collapse in a heap when love doesn’t work out. Also: what to wear, what to cook, and what to buy an overconfident but ultimately appealing sixteen-year-old boy for his birthday (a bicycle bell).

The novel begins with Katherine, a nice, conventionally brought-up, middle-class girl, falling in with her professor’s family, so different from her own. There is such a great number of them, to begin with. There is Jacob, the Marxist professor with the ridiculously hairy chest, and Jane, his beautiful, posh wife, who both loves and resents being the mother of six wild children. There are the six wild children, particularly the two eldest boys, Roger and Jonathan, who play different but almost equally significant roles in Katherine’s sentimental education. She is dazzled by the whole family, who are loud and combative and madly sophisticated without being pompous about it or even seeming to set much store by it (“ ‘I’ll tell you something you’ll hate, shall I?’ I said to him. ‘You’re cultured … You always were,’ ” gives some idea of the attitude). Books and music and politics and sex and money are all discussed at maximum volume over dinner. It stops Katherine in her suburban tracks. Her life is never the same.

I spoke to Trapido about Brother of the More Famous Jack at her house, in Oxford. I was thrilled to discover that she speaks exactly like one of her characters: when making me lunch, she asked if I would like “some dear little tomatoes.” We spoke about structuring a novel, hearing someone say fuck for the first time, and being taken for Doris Lessing.

INTERVIEWER

Could you picture the shape of the book before you started writing it?

BARBARA TRAPIDO

No. You see, I saw no shape. The book is entirely character-based. It progresses via vivid dialogue. Story-wise, it’s simply one episode after another. I began to write it because a friend goaded me. I was chattering out some anecdote and she said, “Tell you what gets on my nerves about you. You dissipate your talent by just talking out stories.” I was a bit stung by this because I thought I’d already been working quite hard, schlepping on two buses, from Durham to the Sunderland Docklands, where I worked and taught. She suggested that I write a story for the Guardian short-story competition. In the end I said I’d give it a go.

Having dreamt up the Goldman family, I couldn’t get enough of them. I kept being drawn back in. I was wanting all the people in my life to go away and get on. I’d wait till the middle of the night and then creep into this little hide. I didn’t tell anyone what I was doing. My husband, Stanley, believed I was finishing my thesis on the Pre-Raphaelite poets and instead I was getting high on inventing dialogue. So no, I didn’t see any shape for it. I just thought, Well, today they can go to the beach and then they can go to the cinema. I played around with the dialogue and made it shorter and tighter and even sometimes made shapes on the page with it. I had no idea what I was writing, though I quickly realized it wasn’t a short story.

After a while, I recalled that it was something I used to do in childhood—invent people, sometimes write little stories, and think, This is just playing and it’s the best fun. I couldn’t stop doing it. It was only once I’d written quite a bit of it that I thought, Is this a soap opera? What am I doing, and has it got any shape? What’s going to happen to these people? That led to a sort of shape. In hindsight, I realized—and the writing was all entirely intuitive, I didn’t plan any of it—that I’d made a few linking threads of imagery to compensate. The repeating references to Monteverdi, the “Hamlet hat,” the older Goldman boy’s initials, appearing and re-appearing in upper case, the embroidered butterfly, the falsetto singing—threads of imagery to weave the novel together. What drives it forward is the energy of its quick-fire dialogue and the wish to keep company with the characters. That is what makes it readable. I’m surprised if people think that it has much in the way of a shape.

INTERVIEWER

Where does the character of Katherine come from? Where does Jacob come from?

TRAPIDO

All the characters came out of the back of my head. None of them are based on real-life people. I find in general that any characters in my books who are real-life people, usually walk-on parts, come out two-dimensional, unlike the imaginary ones. With Katherine, I recalled from my own youth that heady feeling of leaving one’s school days behind, anticipating university, the freedom of being a grown-up.

Jacob and Jane are both wholly unlike anyone I knew. But from my own parents I had a blueprint for a cross-cultural marriage. My dad was more dominant, having gotten where he was via his brain. He grew up dirt-poor and went to Leiden University, in the Netherlands, on one of only eight scholarships that I believe existed at the time. My mum had come from a rather sheltered, calm, bourgeois Berlin household, with holiday homes and skiing in the mountains and a boat on the Wannsee. Her family led sweet, quiet, uneventful lives. They watched the coming of Germany’s fascist dictator with great unease and lost everything as a result of the Second World War. She was very timid and not remotely like Jane, except that she played the piano. Both of my parents were “displaced foreigners” in Cape Town, you might say.

In general, the characters in Jack are all imagined, archetypal. I suppose I invented them because I wanted some exciting pretend friends. I think I enjoyed their shoutiness. Katherine’s sewing and obsession with clothes was totally me at that age, forever at the sewing machine with those Vogue “Paris Original” patterns, and getting corrugations in my skull from sleeping in rollers every night to achieve the right undulations in my dead-straight hair.

INTERVIEWER

I’d like to ask you about the preface to Jacob’s book, which appears at the start of the novel.

TRAPIDO

I so enjoyed inventing that. In fact, I was one of those bloody wives who edited and annotated, not only for my husband, but for quite a few academic types who tend to write in paragraph-long sentences.

INTERVIEWER

Katherine says that this preface influenced the paths that she chooses to tread. How do you see that happening in the novel?

TRAPIDO

She learns a whole different way of negotiating family life. In a way, the book reads like a seventies pamphlet on progressive child-rearing. And it’s very liberated in that it involves interactions between people with less inhibition about being respectable and tidy. It’s also a bit of an examination of social class, the different pockets of middle-class life … And of course, I am an outsider, which makes one a bit more of an anthropologist in the way she looks at society.

INTERVIEWER

How do you think that comes through in the novel, your being anthropological?

TRAPIDO

There’s quite an awareness of social class. I think, in general, I’m completely politically obsessed, addicted to newsprint, like Jake.

We once had a lovely lodger who played the piano, a librarian at the Bodleian Library, a rather effete boy called James, who managed to wedge a small grand piano into our little basement studio flat. This was at the time when the Labour Party was trying to supplant Ken Livingstone and impose poor old Frank Dobson in his place as the mayoral candidate—big news day-to-day at the time. “Who’s Ken Livingstone?” James asked me one day, during one of my rants. I thought, I am so envious of you. You don’t have to waste your days fretting about what’s going on, whether it’s the German election or the Labour Party. You are free to think about Dutch landscape paintings and playing the piano.

INTERVIEWER

Do you think Katherine’s political?

TRAPIDO

I think she probably becomes so as a result of the Goldmans. Jane says that Jacob’s so obsessed with newsprint that if he’s away from his copy of the Guardian, he’ll look through old chest drawers to see if they’ve been lined with two-year-old issues of the Hampstead and Highgate Gazette.

I suppose it’s interesting how quite a lot of English graduates are totally unaware of social class and socioeconomic context. I remember an English fellow, a graduate student, saying, “But it’s got nothing to do with Wordsworth.” And I thought, But of course it has! The socioeconomic context in which these people grow up and survive—you need to know that in order to appreciate the way that the verse kind of explodes. The times through which these people were living impinges on the way they think and write.

INTERVIEWER

Did you show the novel to your husband or did you keep it to yourself?

TRAPIDO

No. I read bits to my teenage daughter, who relished it. I gave Stan the completed proof copy only after it was accepted. I read him the first chapter and he said, “Hey, this is good!” All throughout my secret scribblings, he’d say, “I don’t know what you’re doing, but why don’t you finish your thesis?” Which thankfully ended up turning into papier-mâché in a cardboard box.

The book is very talky. I do like that. I read everything aloud. I write it up by hand. Then I think, Oh God, that’s terrible. I do massive scribbled amendments, read it aloud again—and again. Then I tape-record it and I play it back to myself and I talk some more into the mirror. It’s a sort of staging. And, rather than plotting, what I do is a kind of choreography. I’ll think, Okay, there’s a dining table, this person’s sitting here, and that person’s sitting there. I’ll move myself around, changing chairs, doing dialogue. I’ll be this person, then that person.

INTERVIEWER

As in, you’ll move from one side of the table to the other?

TRAPIDO

Yeah. Or on a train, I’ll determine which way they’re facing. It’s quite hard working out chronology and such things as, Is the season right for them to be eating this or that? Can I get this person on a train from one place to another place before closing time? All that can be a bit of a headache.

But the book is quite polished, because I’d been working it more than for a decade, playing with it. Then one of my friends who was typesetting for Gollancz suggested I submit it. I thought, Oh yeah, Gollancz published all those left book-club books that Jake’s shelves were full of. Maybe they’d like mine. They wrote back within the week saying, “We love your novel. We’d like to publish it. Tell us who you are.” Doris Lessing had just conned a publisher by sending in a manuscript under another name. They thought maybe I was someone a bit experienced who was wanting to make an idiot of them. Well, it was a ten-years-being-polished first novel, so in a sense maybe I was quite “experienced.”

My editor changed nothing except for my spelling of righteous—and she added three commas. I remember this very nice posh girl editor phoning me one day, saying, “Barbara, shouldn’t it be, ‘Fuck off’ comma ‘you old cow?’ ” I remember the very first time somebody said fuck in front of me …

INTERVIEWER

How old were you?

TRAPIDO

I was about twenty-one. It was a Dutch poet who had come to stay.

INTERVIEWER

Does Katherine …

TRAPIDO

She doesn’t. And neither does Jane. They don’t use bad language. But the boys do.

INTERVIEWER

Yes.

TRAPIDO

One woman who reviewed my book said, “This is a book in which the women smile and knit and the men have all the good lines.”

INTERVIEWER

I don’t think that’s true.

TRAPIDO

I think, actually, it is, because the women are more confident, in a way. They don’t need to be shouting and showing off. Though Katherine as the storyteller has some good lines.

INTERVIEWER

Who did you think of as an influence when you were writing?

TRAPIDO

I wasn’t conscious of anybody, really. And I do get so tired of the way nearly every woman writer says, “Oh, Jane Austen was my influence.” I think the one thing I maybe got from Jane Austen is the energy, the way the dialogue dances and sparkles. The first thing one of my friends who read it said was, “You don’t waste any time on the scenery, do you?” Maybe I got that from Jane Austen, the way that she’ll just bounce into, “My dear Mr. Bennet …” I remembered, as a child, how I quite often just skipped bits that you thought of as “description.” With Jack, I evidently just dispensed with the description.

One novel that I suppose was buried in the back of my mind was Iris Murdoch’s first, Under the Net, which I came across when I was sixteen. It’s so theatrical. It ends with a film set that’s collapsing and these two guys who’ve lost their rental and are wandering about London, not knowing quite what to do. They sort of map London, walking around, over Vauxhall Bridge, visiting this person and that. When I read it, I just thought, I love these people. I want to join them. These are my people. I want to be with them crossing Vauxhall Bridge.

Another is a book that my school friend Sue flung at me when I was a bit older, probably eighteen—The Dud Avocado, by Elaine Dundy.

INTERVIEWER

You wrote Brother of the More Famous Jack when you were forty. Did you always think you’d end up writing books?

TRAPIDO

I don’t think I ever had any clear ambitions, being a dreamy, dozy, unmotivated younger sister. Though, thinking back, all through my childhood and adolescence I wrote stories—for my mother, for friends’ children. I didn’t think of it as something I could “market.” With Brother of the More Famous Jack, I rewrote and edited madly at around age forty, but I’d started it a decade earlier. When we left Durham for Oxford, in 1970, I’d put it in a box and forgotten about it, then was pretty preoccupied for the next decade with childcare and part-time teaching. I hauled the box out of the attic when triggered by one of my son’s playgroup friends’ mothers around 1980 and finished it as a sort of serial for her. I rediscovered it as that same blissful sort of playing I mentioned earlier. I couldn’t stop. I never thought of it as something I’d publish.

Rosa Lyster is a writer who lives in London. She previously interviewed the author Laura B. McGrath for our website.

entries.title: At Festival America, France’s America-Themed Literary Festival
entries.summary: “He reads Maurice Blanchot, and he’s got thirteen guns.”
entries.content:
Noelle Mateer

Dispatch

This summer, Festival America, a four-day event that is not in America, released its trailer—a supercut of iconic imagery spanning the history of the United States. Native American men riding horses. A portrait of George Washington. The site of the 1890 Wounded Knee Massacre. Men digging a mass grave. Suffragists parading. Troops storming Normandy. A mushroom cloud. A rocket launch. And text:

Littérature.

Expositions.

60 autrices et auteurs américains.

Next came the headshots of John Grisham and Joyce Carol Oates, Laura Kasischke and Ta-Nehisi Coates, superimposed over scenes from the March on Washington. Next, a ticker tape of sixty names, one of them my husband’s, scrolled across footage of men marching into war. The mostly black-and-white montage switched into color as Ronald Reagan signed a bill and a plane smashed into the Twin Towers.

Festival America, which is held every two years, typically invites authors from across the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean whose works have recently been translated into French for a series of panels and workshops in Vincennes, a town just outside Paris. But the 2026 lineup was 100 percent from the U.S.A. in honor of the country’s semiquincentennial. Among those invited were Alison Bechdel, Tommy Orange, Viet Thanh Nguyen, Karen Russell, Patrick Radden Keefe, and many more of our nation’s best-known working writers, plus my husband, Jake, who was suffering from an acute case of impostor syndrome.

To say Jake was surprised to be included in this lineup is an understatement. His debut novel, Slime Line, was published so quietly by a university press that when he signed with a larger imprint in New York for his next book, his editor still referred to him as a “debut author.” Nevertheless, a major French publisher acquired Slime Line—or as it’s known in French, Alaska Parano—and two years after its U.S. release, we flew from Pennsylvania to Paris to find that he’d amassed a not-insubstantial Francophone following. His book was front and center on the NEW AND NOTABLE table at the bookstore near our hotel. It was there, too, at a bookstore on the next block. And guess who was a STAFF PICK at Shakespeare and Company.

Jake was beside himself with a confused sort of glee. The fawning messages he’d received from French-language accounts on Instagram were beginning to make sense. One post praised his novel—which is based on his experience working in the commercial-fishing industry—for being a beautiful treatise on the “solidarity of magnificent losers.”

Around this time his French publicist reached out. She wanted to know if he would speak to a journalist at a major French magazine for a profile as the “new voice of America.” Evidence was mounting that Jake’s work was touching a very specific French sensibility. In Vincennes, I made it my mission to find out what.

*

That’s not exactly true. That’s just something journalists say to end their opener with a little narrative thrust. Getting to the bottom of French literary sensibilities was more of a secondary reason for me, trailing wine and cheese. On the festival’s first full day, authors and their plus-ones were invited to a “cocktail lunch” at the Château de Vincennes, the seat of French kings from the fourteenth through the seventeenth centuries. There, we chewed on skewered radish slices, thin breads topped with charcuterie, and pert meringues in the shadow of the tallest donjon in Europe.

Over drinks, I asked the festival’s head interpreter if there was any historical torture equipment around. She told me that the most terrible death at the château had less to do with torture than with disease. During the Hundred Years’ War, King Henry V of England had retreated there shortly after the Siege of Meaux. He’d just conquered Normandy and was near to becoming king of France. But the man barely had time to settle into his new digs before he got dysentery and died. That was in 1422.

Observing the United States’s birthday in Europe is a reminder that we have a minuscule history—a cultural handicap that our literature must overcome. “Compared to Europe,” the festival’s founder, Francis Geffard, told me, “it’s very recent.” Nevertheless, two hundred fifty is a pleasingly round number, and he saw “a good occasion” to make this year’s festival about the U.S. It also allowed him to pursue what might seem like a lofty goal: to assemble enough American authors, spanning generations, geographies, and identities, to see once and for all “what American fiction has to say to readers outside of America.”

This seems like an impossible task until you remember the one thing that unites American writers, old and young, established and emerging: they will nearly always accept a free trip to Paris. As Francis told me, “It is very unusual for a writer to turn down the invitation.”

*

After cocktail lunch, Francis was moderating “The French Taste for American Literature,” a roundtable with three Francophone experts on American letters, at the Hôtel de Ville, Vincennes’s nineteenth-century town hall. To enter the building, I had first to walk along a red carpet, flanked by a photography exhibition featuring, among others, an image of terrified migrants paddling across the Rio Grande. Inside, more than two hundred people had climbed the grand staircase to the marriage hall, where frescoed aristocrats looked down from the walls. The previous festival had drawn sixty thousand people—the press team didn’t seem to think this year’s turnout would be any less.

This was a French-language panel, and Francis’s questions hinted at certain shared assumptions among French readers. “We agree that American writers aren’t quite the same as, say, French writers,” began one. “From France, we often tend to imagine the United States as a country without culture,” began another.

One of the panelists was Sébastien Bonifay, a Corsican writer and bookseller who traveled to the U.S. more than twenty times to visit his favorite American authors at their homes, often for days at a time. His recent book, (Not) Born in the USA, recounts meetings with James Ellroy, Chris Offutt, Donald Ray Pollock, Stuart Dybek, James McBride, and more. These are known names, if not exactly those an American would pick. “The literature that nourishes me,” he said, “is an American literature that Americans don’t like.”

He called it “a literature of the margins,” and panelists riffed on what those rough edges were. One placed marginal American literature in a lineage of countercultures that rail against l’establishment (anglicism, pejorative)—rock and roll, psychedelia, punk. Another said that the United States has two literatures: one of “the coasts” and one of “the other,” rarely published but often excellent. This thrilling literature of the margins was often published by universities, which, the panelist said, “have wonderful presses.” It didn’t matter that this type of book didn’t always achieve mainstream acclaim; the panelists seemed to trust their own taste.

The more the panelists riffed, the more they came to describe my husband. A panelist brought up the idea of “an American-style résumé”—belonging, it seemed, to someone who fits writing in between blue-collar gigs. The panelists called this type of writer “artisanal,” someone “whose real-life experience shows through in their work.” This writer “had lived.” And this writer had done so in places the French reader could hardly imagine, like Ohio.

It’s in this misunderstood land that Sébastien begins his book: in a Wendy’s parking lot, sweating with anxiety about his impending visit to Donald Ray Pollock’s house. After the panel, I found Sébastien sitting behind a stack of copies in the book-signing tent, and he told me he fell in love with American literature at fourteen, reading Stephen King. It wasn’t the horror that gripped him; it was the way King described small American towns. Before a single plot twist even dropped, Sébastien was entranced by Derry, King’s fictional Maine hamlet. This pleased me, as someone from an American town.

“The writers who have a lot of success in France,” he said, often aren’t as successful at home, and sometimes “are not even published in America.” I asked him why French people liked American literature that doesn’t get much attention in the U.S. He had a theory about this. “French people, they’ve got a problem with America,” he said. “We are fascinated by America. But we truly, deeply think we should be, as France, as a country, where America is.”

For one, France has so much more history, whereas the history of the United States is terribly short. That’s why many of the American books that become popular in France show America’s darker, shittier, seedier side. He pointed to Benjamin Whitmer, an American writer whose noirs have a much larger audience in France. Sébastien visited Whitmer in Colorado as part of his series of pilgrimages to the United States.

“This guy has got thirteen guns,” Sébastien told me. French people think owning a gun means you’re a redneck, he said. But when Sébastien visited him in Colorado, Whitmer asked him about Maurice Blanchot. “Maurice Blanchot!” The fact that someone could own thirteen guns and be a fan of the French literary theorist Maurice Blanchot was significant enough to warrant repetition. “Benjamin Whitmer knows Maurice Blanchot,” he said. “He reads Maurice Blanchot, and he’s got thirteen guns.” He moved his fist emphatically, then clarified. “One of them is for the grizzlies. One of them is for the coyotes.”

To Sébastien, Whitmer was one kind of writer, to be juxtaposed against another. “It’s just my opinion, but these writers are a lot better than the other ones,” he said. “Really, I don’t care about Jeffrey Eugenides! Really, I don’t care.”

*

Elsewhere in the bookselling tent, Jake, the proud author of a title published by West Virginia University Press, was already flying through book sales. He had just spoken to a class of teens who had mobbed him like a rock star. When I told him about Sébastien, he said, “That guy rules. I think he wants us to come to Corsica.”

A long queue for Joyce Maynard snaked around the booths. I introduced myself to two women thumbing through books, asking them what they liked about American literature. “The stories, the journey, the wide-open spaces, and all that,” said the younger one, who quickly turned her own questions on me. They had come here to learn about America, and here I was, a real, live American. At their prodding, I told them about my husband’s work.

“Ah, that wouldn’t exist here, someone who writes about being a fisherman,” the woman said. “In France, it’s more l’establishment.”

I asked what she meant by l’establishment.

“Professionals,” her companion clarified. “I thought your husband would be more like a banker, to be writing about capitalism.”

To understand French literature today, the younger went on, I ought to consider the woman in the black hat with the red lipstick. “She has her own myth,” the older woman said.

I’ll confess that at this point, I assumed my French was failing me. The older woman had just made a point about le wokisme that I couldn’t quite follow and, out of fear, didn’t ask her to clarify. But I looked up the lady with the black hat and red lipstick later, and it turns out they were speaking about Amélie Nothomb, a Belgian-Francophone novelist with a penchant for wearing large hats and appearing on TV. She was named a baroness by King Philippe.

There seemed to be all sorts of fashionable characters floating around the French literary world. The novelist Rob Franklin told me he was at the festival’s opening ceremony when an older woman named Sophie introduced herself to him. She was around ninety and striking, with a pixie cut and an eccentric style. Rob had been told that his French editor was named Sophie. This woman asked if she could take his picture. “I was like, ‘Okay, sure. My publisher wants to take my photo,’ ” he told me. Sophie pulled out a monocle to look at her schedule. Then she did a portrait session with him.

The next day, Rob went to meet Sophie at his publisher’s tent. It was a different woman. He spent the festival wondering who the hell had taken his photo until the last day, when Sophie No. 1 found him again and handed him her business card. It turned out she was France’s most famous photographer of writers, and she’d been doing it for sixty years. “I found out she’s like … quite famous,” he told me. On her card was a black-and-white portrait she’d taken of Michel Foucault.

*

There was one person I wanted to ask about the word l’establishment: Fabienne Gondrand, a literary translator who served as Jake’s interpreter throughout the festival. Fabienne had sat beside him on panels, repeating his comments in French. I told Fabienne that a few people had used this word with me to pinpoint the differences between French and American contemporary literature. I wondered if she, too, thought American writers were more anti-l’establishment.

“That’s a little reductive,” she said, seeming surprised. She thought perhaps the people I’d spoken to had used that word because the festival had done a good job curating diverse voices, such as nonwhite and Indigenous writers whose works explicitly challenge American cultural norms. It occurred to me that I had perhaps oversimplified what French readers had intended l’establishment to mean. I’d developed a self-serving theory that the writing world consisted of two camps (coastal literati and scrappy Rust Belt writers with jobs) and that in France, everyone recognized the latter as superior. This is silly, when l’establishment is so obviously not writers in major metro areas with big book deals. L’establishment américain, really, had been invited and declined. I’m talking about Charles Kushner.

At every edition of Festival America since 2002, Francis told me, the U.S. ambassador to France has given a speech on opening night. Currently, that position is held by Kushner, the real-estate developer and pardoned felon. The U.S. Embassy typically forks over a little cultural funding for the festival—less than the Canadian embassy, but not nothing—and this year they slashed their contribution by 80 percent. Francis took this as a sign of distrust and refused the embassy’s money altogether.

Francis told me that French people “are feeling a little estranged” from the U.S. at the moment. Shortly after we spoke, Festival America distributed a press release with sharper wording. “Ironically,” it said, this funding cut had occurred during “the very year of the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence,” when the festival was hosting the largest delegation of American writers ever “in our country, and likely in Europe or anywhere else.”

The festival is right to point out the rarity of this delegation, as these writers would rarely be grouped together. On home turf, they’d more likely be gathered by subject matter, identity, or genre, because in the U.S., “American” is not a uniting descriptor—we’re too close to see clearly. But in Vincennes, we can step back and see the whole picture. What struck me about French readers was their confidence in their own taste, in how it could supersede that of most American readers. But French people have been gazing upon America their whole lives. When I returned from the festival, I found myself in a rare moment of America gazing back. Kushner’s embassy was advising Americans to “exercise caution.” Since the festival, student protests there have erupted into widespread riots, and I think we could safely say those were aimed at l’establishment.

entries.title: Robert Caro, Unlocked: The Better Our Country Will Be
entries.summary: To celebrate the results of the midterm elections, we’ve unlocked Robert Caro’s Art of Biography interview and Matthew Baker’s short story “Why Visit America” from the archive.
entries.content:
Hazel Byers

Redux

Each week, The Paris Review unlocks stories, poems, and interviews from our archive for our readers. This week, we’ve unlocked Robert Caro’s Art of Biography interview, along with Matthew Baker’s short story “Why Visit America,” from the archive.

At a town hall meeting, the residents of Plainsfield, Texas, the fictional town featured in Matthew Baker’s story “Why Visit America,” vote unanimously to secede from the United States. They call their new nation “America.”

“We were fed up with our country,” writes Baker in issue no. 230 of the Review. “The executives were busy making donations that funded the campaigns of the politicians, the politicians were busy passing laws that protected the interests of the executives, and pretty much nothing else seemed to be getting done. We were antigovernment, we were anticorporate, but mostly we were normal people who couldn’t afford to buy an election and had come to understand that our votes didn’t mean shit.”

Several of us at the Review returned to Baker’s story after last week’s midterm elections yielded once-unthinkable results, including in Texas, where Democrats won their first Senate seat since 1988, their first governorship since 1995, and control over the state House for the first time in more than two decades.

“We live in a democracy, so ultimately, even despite a Robert Moses, a lot of political power comes from our votes,” says Robert Caro in his Art of Biography interview, published in issue no. 216 of the Review. “The more we understand about the realities of the political process, the better informed our votes will be. And then, presumably, in some very diffuse, very inchoate way, the better our country will be.”

This week, to celebrate, we’ve unlocked Caro’s interview and Baker’s “Why Visit America” from the archive.

INTERVIEW

The Art of Biography No. 5

Robert Caro

CARO

I thought, There’s one guy who’s with Lyndon Johnson most of the day, and it’s not his campaign manager, it’s his chauffeur! Because in the Texas Hill Country, a lot of anything is driving—that’s ninety percent of the time. His chauffeur was a guy named Carroll Keach. He lived in some place outside Corpus Christi, and it was hard to get to. It was, like, a 180-mile drive or something. But I kept going back to him.

He wasn’t a loquacious Texan, he was a laconic Texan. I would ask, What was Johnson doing between campaign stops? And he would say something like, Oh, he was just sitting there in the backseat. I just had to keep asking him questions. I mean, you’re driving, Carroll, and Lyndon Johnson is in the backseat? What was he doing in the backseat? Finally, he told me that Johnson often would be talking to himself. So I’d call and say, Carroll, when you said he was talking to himself, what was he saying? Finally, Carroll told me, It was like he was having discussions with himself about whether he had had a successful day, and if he had made a good impression on voters or not. So I’d say, What do you mean by that? How do you know that’s what he was talking about?

From issue no. 216 (Spring 2016)

PROSE

Why Visit America

Matthew Baker

There wasn’t anything special about us. We were just an average town. Porch swings, wading pools, split rail fences, pump jacks bobbing for oil on the horizon. Meetings at town hall were well attended, sure, but we weren’t some hotbed of insurgents. We didn’t subscribe to any one brand of politics. We couldn’t even be plotted onto your basic left/right binary. Our town had everything: pro-lifers who supported gay marriage, pro-choicers who opposed gay marriage, climate change deniers who owned solar panels, universal health care campaigners who preferred private insurance, creationists with degrees in biology and geology, loyal conservatives, staunch liberals, moderates, radicals, and ornery retirees whose only real issue was guns. And yet that winter we found ourselves united by a common sentiment.

From issue no. 230 (Fall 2019)

Hazel Byers is the Review’s engagement editor.
